title: Augustine and Pelagius
hookLine: can we be good without grace? Augustine said no; Pelagius was judged to say yes

cards: One short line in a prayer started a long quarrel. In his Confessions, Augustine says to God, more or less: give what you command, and then command whatever you will.
If you want me to be good, you'll have to give me the goodness first. Augustine himself later wrote that a monk named Pelagius, said to have come from Britain, heard that line and couldn't stand it.
To Pelagius it sounded like an excuse, as if people could sit back and wait for God to make them good. Their argument filled books. Today: Augustine and Pelagius.

teach.h: CAN WE BE GOOD WITHOUT GRACE?
teach.b: The question underneath is simple to ask: can a person be good without grace? Grace, here, means God's help, freely given, not earned.

teach.h: PELAGIUS: GOD COMMANDS, WE CAN OBEY.
teach.b: Pelagius was a serious man who wanted Christians to live what they said they believed. God gave us free will and the commandments, he argued, and God doesn't command the impossible.
So we can obey, and we're responsible when we don't. When he spoke of grace, he pointed to gifts already given: our nature, the law, the example of Jesus. Augustine saw a wound left untreated.

teach.h: AUGUSTINE: THE WILL ITSELF NEEDS HEALING.
teach.b: In his reading, the human will itself is bent, and a bent will can't straighten itself any more than a broken leg can set itself.
So grace has to come first, not as a reward for trying, but as the healing that makes trying possible. He leaned on Jesus's words in John's Gospel: "for without me ye can do nothing."
Church councils sided with Augustine, and Pelagius's teaching was condemned.

Some historians think Pelagius was more careful than his opponents made him sound, since some of his words reach us through their quotations: worth remembering whenever the winners of an argument describe the losers.
And Paul gave both men a verse to hold.

teach.h: WORK IT OUT; GOD WORKS IN YOU.
teach.b: Philippians: "work out your own salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do." Churches still balance those two sentences differently.
But the West's answer, after that long argument, was grace first.

how: Western churches, Catholic and Protestant, teach that God's grace comes before any good a person does, following Augustine against Pelagius, and some Christians pray for help before beginning a task or a day's work.

o: a debate over who should lead the church in Rome
two monks arguing over the date of Easter
an old quarrel over being good without grace

games.q: you're Pelagius, and you hear Augustine's prayer: give what you command, and command what you will. what's your worry?
o: that it's too long to memorize.
that people will wait for God to make them good, and stop trying.
that it sounds too much like the creed.
games.why: Pelagius feared it sounded like an excuse. Augustine answered that grace doesn't stop trying; it makes trying possible.

practice: Think of one thing waiting for you today that you'd rather avoid, a hard email, a dull chore, a conversation you've put off, and notice how much of you wants to do it well and how much doesn't.
If you pray, you can ask God for help with that one task, by name. If you don't, notice that you won't do it entirely on your own: someone taught you, someone fed you, something got you this far.

wordCard.voice: Augustine and Pelagius. An old argument over whether people can be good without grace. Pelagius stressed our power to obey; Augustine said grace must come first.

orig.note: Greek: grace, favor, a gift freely given. The New Testament word behind the argument.

carryVoice: Your line: grace first. The healing comes before the trying. Until tomorrow.
